The mission

Honest numbers in a world of scale creep

I got tired of printing miniatures that did not match the label. So I built a tool that does the math for you — and I update it when the community tells me I got something wrong.

"32mm" means nothing

If you have been in this hobby for more than a week, you have seen it. You download a "32mm" miniature, print it, and it towers over your "28mm" army. Or it looks like a child next to a tank that was supposedly "1:56."

We call this scale creep. Every sculptor measures differently. Some go to the top of the head, some to the eyes. Some account for base thickness, some do not. For anyone trying to build a coherent collection, it is a mess of wasted resin and failed prints.

I have thrown away enough resin to know. That is why I started measuring everything with digital calipers.

The 175cm baseline

I built STLACCESS in a bedroom workshop. I realized that while "28mm" is a marketing term, "1:56" is a mathematical ratio. To bridge the gap, I needed a fixed point.

I settled on the 175cm human baseline because it is what most of the hobby uses, as far as I can tell. By assuming a standard human height of 1.75 meters, I can calculate how large a model should be in any ratio or system scale.

Eye level (160cm)

The standard for fantasy and sci-fi miniatures. Measures to the eyes, not the crown, because helmets and headgear vary. A 175cm human has eyes at 160cm.

Top of head (175cm)

The standard for historical military kits and display busts where realism matters. Total height from feet to crown.

Why this works

The 175cm baseline is arbitrary but consistent. It does not matter if the "average" human is 170cm or 180cm in real life. What matters is that every conversion on this site uses the same starting point, so the ratios between scales are mathematically sound. A 28mm to 32mm conversion is 114.3% whether your reference human is 175cm or 185cm. The baseline just gives us a common language.

How I test the numbers

Math on a spreadsheet is not enough. I print test pieces and measure them with Mitutoyo Absolute digital calipers (0.01mm resolution). Here is what I have learned from my own prints:

Resin shrinkage

Standard grey resins shrink 0.8% to 1.5% after UV curing. Water-washable resins shrink more (up to 2%). I add 1% to my resin recommendations because that is what matches my measurements.

FDM accuracy

FDM does not shrink like resin, but over-extrusion can add 0.3% to 0.5% to dimensions. I calibrate e-steps on every machine before I test.

Layer height bias

At 0.05mm layer height, a 28mm model has 560 layers. At 0.1mm, it has 280. The coarser layer height can create a 0.1-0.2mm stair-step error on curved surfaces.

I test on multiple machines because not everyone has a Bambu Lab. The percentages work on Elegoo Saturn 3, Anycubic Photon Mono X, Prusa MK4, and Creality Ender 3. If a number fails on a specific machine, I note it in the reference library.

From a 40 euro printer to calipers

I started with an Easythreed printer from AliExpress. It cost 40 euros, sounded like a coffee grinder, and taught me about precision the hard way. Prints warped, dimensions were wrong, and I had no idea why.

Now I run a Bambu Lab X1 Carbon with AMS. The leap from budget to high-end showed me what is possible when the machine does what the slicer says. But I have not forgotten the struggle. Most people do not have a Bambu Lab. That is why every percentage on this site is tested on entry-level machines too.

I have also learned that expensive resin does not mean accurate resin. Some of the worst shrinkage I measured came from premium-brand water-washable resin. The cheap standard grey from Elegoo was more predictable. I note resin-specific offsets where they matter.

What STLACCESS is

It is a tool I built for myself. I do not sell STL files, resin, or printers. There are no affiliate links. It is free because I needed it and figured others did too.

The numbers come from my prints. I calculate them, I print them, I measure them. If you submit a correction through the reference pages, I test it on my machines before updating. If enough people tell me the same thing, I change it. That is the deal.

It is never finished. New scales appear every year. New games use different baselines. I update the library when I find discrepancies or when manufacturers change their sculpting standards. If something looks wrong on your table, send it in.

Stop guessing. Start printing.
